method: Solve all three bound modern prompts from physical reasoning; write this file before reading either candidate answer. No earlier answer, source-text, plate or figure review supplies an answer verdict.

solutions.physicalModel: Absolute refractive index of a transparent medium at a specified optical frequency and a fixed state of that medium: n = c / v_phase, where c is the vacuum speed of light and v_phase is the phase velocity in the medium.
reasoning: The absolute index compares propagation of the same optical frequency in vacuum and in the medium. It is not an angle, an arbitrary degree of bending, or the ratio of frequencies.
For the ordinary transparent media considered here, n greater than 1 means that the phase propagates more slowly than in vacuum; n = 1.5 means v_phase = c / 1.5, not 1.5c.
Frequency and medium state must be specified: dispersion makes the index frequency-dependent, and a medium's physical state can affect its index.
Frequency remains unchanged across a stationary interface. The phase velocity and wavelength change, so a different refractive index does not mean a different optical frequency.
This definition concerns phase velocity, not necessarily pulse/group velocity or information velocity. There is no need to introduce those advanced distinctions into the child's opening answer.
solutions.childReadableAnswerEn: The absolute refractive index tells us how much slower light's phase travels in a medium than in a vacuum. It is n = c/v: divide the vacuum speed c by the phase speed v in the medium. Compare the same frequency and keep the medium's conditions fixed.
translationRequirements: Both languages must identify the vacuum reference and use the ratio c/v in the same direction.
A short speed explanation is acceptable when the phase-velocity, same-frequency and fixed-state interpretation is made explicit nearby.
Neither language may claim that refraction changes frequency or that the index is a universal constant for every colour and condition.

solutions.physicalModel: Ordinary white notebook paper and coloured-pencil marks viewed under white illumination through selectively transmitting red or green glass. Visibility is the brightness contrast of each mark against the filtered paper, not preservation of the mark's original hue.
reasoning: White paper reflects green as well as red light. Through green glass the paper remains relatively bright and green.

The red pencil mark mainly reflects red light and reflects relatively little green. Green glass strongly reduces its red return, so that mark appears dark against the green paper and is easy to distinguish.
The green mark mainly returns the transmitted green light. Its brightness contrast against the filtered paper is reduced, so it is less conspicuous.

Through red glass, the white paper and the red mark both return transmitted red light. That reduces the red mark's contrast, while the green mark becomes dark. Red glass therefore emphasizes the wrong mark.
The left/right arrangement is preserved in the task but does not determine the filter choice.

Real glass is not a perfect filter and coloured pencils do not reflect only one wavelength. The classroom conclusion assumes the usual reasonably selective filters and pigments; darkness and reduced contrast need not mean zero light or complete disappearance.
solutions.childReadableAnswerEn: Use the green glass. The white page still looks bright green, but most of the red light from 'Excellent' is blocked, so that red mark looks dark and stands out. The green 'Good' mark blends more with the green page. Red glass would make the red mark blend with the page instead.
translationRequirements: The chosen filter is green in both languages.
The target remains the handwritten red '优' ('Excellent'); green '良' ('Good') stays to its left.
Clearer means stronger mark-to-paper contrast, not keeping the target red or choosing matching glass.
Do not substitute a luminous screen or emitted coloured letters for reflected light from handwritten marks.

solutions.physicalModel: White light containing a range of wavelengths passes through a dispersive prism and is observed on a screen or in a corresponding optical image. Each wavelength produces a shifted finite-width image of the incoming beam or slit.
reasoning: A prism disperses both narrow and wide white beams: different wavelengths have different refractive indices and therefore different deviations. The beam width does not switch dispersion on or off.
For a sufficiently narrow input, each colour image is narrow compared with the displacement between colour bands being distinguished. The coloured images can therefore be resolved as a spectrum.

A wide input makes each colour image wide. These displaced images overlap heavily across the middle. Light of many colours reaches the same places, which look approximately white when the usual broad white-light beam has substantial spectral overlap.
At the edges the set of overlapping colours is incomplete. Some colour components extend farther than others, so coloured fringes remain visible.
Separation is relative to the beam-image width, prism dispersion, viewing distance and optical resolution. Adjacent infinitesimally close wavelengths are not all completely separated.
Making a slit indefinitely narrower cannot guarantee indefinitely sharper separation: diffraction, finite aperture, aberrations and observation resolution impose practical limits.
Do not assign a universal left/right edge colour without specifying prism orientation. For ordinary normal dispersion violet is deviated more than red, but the screen orientation is not bound here.
solutions.childReadableAnswerEn: The prism spreads different colours in different directions. A narrow beam gives narrow colour images, so we can see them apart. A wide beam gives wide colour images that overlap in the middle and mix to look nearly white. At the edges they do not all overlap, so colour is visible there. 'Narrow enough' depends on the prism and the viewing setup; real instruments cannot separate every nearby wavelength perfectly.
translationRequirements: Both languages must explain wavelength-dependent deviation and finite-width colour-image overlap.
Neither language may say a wide beam is not dispersed, is made of fewer colours, or makes no spectrum in any sense.
Central whiteness is the ordinary overlapping white-light case, not a universal exact-colour law.
The practical resolution limitation must survive translation; arbitrarily narrow beams do not guarantee perfect separation.
